subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 34-year-old woman with a 2-year history of sarcoidosis presents with fatigue, confusion, polyuria, and constipation. She takes no calcium or vitamin D supplements. Examination shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and dry mucous membranes. Laboratory studies show calcium 12.4 mg/dL, phosphate 3.1 mg/dL, parathyroid hormone suppressed to 6 pg/mL, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D elevated at 96 pg/mL.
question: Which of the following best explains the hypercalcemia in this patient?

options.text: Ectopic parathyroid hormone secretion by granulomas
Parathyroid hormone-related peptide secretion by a carcinoma

explanation_correct: In granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis, epithelioid macrophages express 1-alpha-hydroxylase that is not regulated by parathyroid hormone or by feedback inhibition. These cells convert circulating 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol outside the kidney, increasing intestinal calcium absorption and bone resorption, which raises serum calcium and suppresses parathyroid hormone.

explanation_incorrect.A: Parathyroid hormone is suppressed, not elevated, in this patient; granulomas do not produce parathyroid hormone.
explanation_incorrect.B: Bone metastases would produce a high parathyroid hormone-related peptide or local osteolysis with an elevated alkaline phosphatase and focal bone lesions, and would not raise 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
explanation_incorrect.C: Primary hyperparathyroidism raises both calcium and parathyroid hormone; here parathyroid hormone is appropriately suppressed by the high calcium.
explanation_incorrect.E: Parathyroid hormone-related peptide secretion (humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy) elevates calcium while lowering 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and would not explain elevated calcitriol.

educationalObjective: Granulomatous diseases cause hypercalcemia through extrarenal, unregulated 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity in macrophages that produces excess calcitriol.
